research.summary:
It's real: at Colosseum World's Fair, a standalone off-chain game would score badly. Four sources point the same way.

(1) The official rules (PDF, text extracted locally) give six criteria. One is "UX: How well does this Project Submission utilize blockchain to create great UX for downstream users?" Every sponsor track is worded as "the best products that integrate with the X blockchain".

(2) colosseum.com/hackathon says work is "judged only on the work completed between the competition's start and end dates". That window is Sep 14 to Oct 12, 2026, and past development must be disclosed.

(3) Colosseum's own advice says to "enable new markets that couldn't exist without crypto". It lists "Failing to explain Solana integration clearly" as a common pitfall, and says judges examine "on-chain logic".

(4) I checked all 26 gaming and consumer winners from Breakout, Radar and Renaissance, plus the Cypherpunk consumer winners. None was a pure off-chain game. The top games are on-chain in play itself: Supersize "fully on-chain", Lana Roads "every hop is a transaction", Block Stranding "all game actions are recorded in real time". Others put token wagers or rewards around the game (Scrim, Barnfight, Legends of the Sun). Cypherpunk (2025) had no gaming winners; its consumer winners were prediction and trading products.

Two corrections to the brief. The Arbitrum track is $25,000 across 5 ($5k each), which matches 5x$5k. The Base track is also 5 x $5k. Tempo is $100,000 across 10.

The track texts don't ask for anything specific. Tempo's resource groups are payments, stablecoins, "data and machine payments", and company formation and banking. So a stablecoin payout that the game itself triggers fits Tempo better than a game with a link to a separate page.

I found no organiser commentary using the words "thin blockchain use", "why crypto" or wallet friction as a judging penalty. The nearest are the "couldn't exist without crypto" line and Codex notes that wallets need to be simpler and embedded wallets cut friction.

Overall this favours building a real on-chain action into the heist during the window, with invisible or embedded wallets, over keeping it standalone.

findings.claim: Official judging criteria include a UX criterion that is explicitly about using blockchain, plus Functionality, Impact, Novelty, Open-source/composability and Business Plan. An off-chain game gets little on the UX and composability criteria.
findings.evidence: Rules s.8: "(d) UX: How well does this Project Submission utilize blockchain to create great UX for downstream users? (e) Open-source: Is this Project Submission open-source? How well does the Project Submission compose with other primitives in the crypto ecosystem?" Source: https://colosseum.com/legal/Crypto%20World's%20Fair%20Hackathon%20Rules.pdf (text extracted locally with pdftotext)

findings.claim: The contest's stated purpose is building with public blockchains.
findings.evidence: Rules s.1: "The objective of the Contest is to leverage public blockchains to build solutions and experiment with blockchain technology." (same PDF)

findings.claim: Sponsor tracks are defined only as products that integrate with the chain. Tempo is 10 prizes from $100k. Arbitrum, Base and Robinhood Chain are each 5 prizes from $25k ($5k each).
findings.evidence: Rules s.14: "(f) Tempo track: $100,000 will be awarded across 10 of the best products that integrate with the Tempo blockchain"; "(j) Base track: $25,000 will be awarded across 5 of the best products that integrate with the Base blockchain"; "(k) Arbitrum track: $25,000 will be awarded across 5 of the best products that integrate with the Arbitrum blockchain". Arbitrum Foundation: "$25,000 across the top 5 startups integrating the Arbitrum blockchain" https://blog.arbitrum.foundation/builders-block-026-300k-awaits-at-founder-house-singapore-what-great-startups-have-in-common/

findings.claim: In-window rule: only work done Sep 14 to Oct 12, 2026 is judged, and past work must be disclosed. The 8 existing heist levels and 73 existing ShelterSplit tests earn little credit by themselves. New integration work inside the window is what gets judged.
findings.evidence: colosseum.com/hackathon: "Teams may begin development before the hackathon, but products are judged only on the work completed between the competition's start and end dates." Builders must "disclose all relevant past development work in the submission form." Rules s.5: "The Contest Period starts at 6:00am PT on September 14, 2026 and ends at 11:59pm PT on October 12, 2026." https://colosseum.com/hackathon

findings.claim: The official track guidance for Tempo only lists resource themes: payments, stablecoins, machine payments, company formation. There is no gaming guidance. A stablecoin payment triggered from inside the game matches these themes.
findings.evidence: ColosseumOrg/hackathon-resources manifest.json, Tempo resource groups: "Foundations", "Payment applications", "Stablecoins and exchange", "Data and machine payments", "Company formation and banking"; Base: "Application stack", "Payments", "Optional distribution"; Arbitrum: "Build contracts", "Bridge and message", "Test and ship". Sponsor .md descriptions are empty. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ColosseumOrg/hackathon-resources/main/manifest.json

findings.claim: Organiser guidance says products should need crypto.
findings.evidence: "Build products that enable new markets that couldn't exist without crypto or improve existing markets by bringing them onchain" and "Crypto at its core unlocks new markets fueled by digitally-native assets." https://blog.colosseum.com/how-to-win-a-colosseum-hackathon/

findings.claim: Colosseum workshop names weak chain integration as a common pitfall, and judges inspect on-chain logic.
findings.evidence: A common pitfall: "Failing to explain Solana integration clearly." Judges want to understand "how it leverages Solana" and examine "on-chain logic, and overall architecture." Tech demo should be "technical, direct, and specific to implementation". https://blog.colosseum.com/perfecting-your-hackathon-submission/

findings.claim: Judges also weigh a startup's business case and traction: full-time founders, a real problem, traction. Game quality alone doesn't win.
findings.evidence: "there will always be an award for the best public good"; "judges look for evidence that a team is solving a real problem for real users"; pitch video "usually the first item judges review and can determine whether a project is shortlisted"; "presentations are required to be under 3 minutes". https://blog.colosseum.com/how-to-win-a-colosseum-hackathon/ and https://blog.colosseum.com/perfecting-your-hackathon-submission/

findings.claim: Radar (2024) gaming winners were all on-chain or token-based. First place Supersize is fully on-chain, with token entry and payout.
findings.evidence: Winners post: Supersize "a fully on-chain high stakes multiplayer game"; The Arena "a PvP social trading game"; Windfall "a game based on leveraging LSTs"; Barnfight "allowing communities to play token-incentivized games together"; Quantro "a PvP ETF trading game". https://blog.colosseum.com/announcing-the-winners-of-the-solana-radar-hackathon/ . Project page: "Supersize is a real-time, fully on-chain, high stakes multiplayer game powered by Magicblock." https://colosseum.com/arena/projects/explore/supersize

findings.claim: Breakout (2025) gaming winners had real on-chain actions in gameplay or wagering. None was a standalone off-chain game.
findings.evidence: Winners post: CFL "a fantasy sports app for crypto tokens"; Scrim "a skill-based wagering platform for competitive gamers"; Block Stranding "the world's first survival OMRPG on Solana"; Lana Roads "an onchain game built using an Ephemeral Rollup"; Huch "lets players to use gaming assets as collateral for crypto loans". https://blog.colosseum.com/announcing-the-winners-of-the-solana-breakout-hackathon/ . Project pages: Lana Roads "where every hop is a transaction" (https://colosseum.com/arena/projects/explore/lana-roads-1); Block Stranding "all game actions are recorded in real time as fast, zero-fee transactions" (https://colosseum.com/arena/projects/explore/block-stranding).

findings.claim: Renaissance (2024) gaming winners were mostly on-chain or reward-bearing. Maneko Pet (Tamagotchi-style) is the closest to a casual game, and the winners post doesn't mention on-chain mechanics for it. I didn't fetch its project page, so this is unverified.
findings.evidence: Meshmap+City Champ "generates 3D scans incentivized by token rewards"; Legends of the Sun "up to 5 friends or foes for rewards"; Mining Badger "an onchain crafting game using Honeycomb Protocol"; Moon Boi Universe "a web3 cyber-fantasy, open-world RPG optimized for mobile"; Maneko Pet "a simple and fun Tamagotchi-style mobile game, complete with a built-in game launcher". https://blog.colosseum.com/announcing-the-winners-of-the-solana-renaissance-hackathon/

findings.claim: Cypherpunk (2025) had no gaming winners. Its consumer winners were financial or tokenised products: prediction markets, a trading chat, socialfi.
findings.evidence: Consumer: Capitola "a prediction markets meta-aggregator"; Superfan "a new a meta-record label for artists and their fans"; Fora "a group chat based trading platform and prediction market protocol"; Toaster.trade "a TikTok-style socialfi platform powered by Hyperliquid and Solana"; Nomu "a marketplace where you can buy products and get rewarded for being early". https://blog.colosseum.com/announcing-the-winners-of-the-solana-cypherpunk-hackathon/

findings.claim: Colosseum's investment theme for games is about deep token/social integration, not off-chain games.
findings.evidence: "After a 2024 boom in memecoins, founders are now exploring deeper integrations of social media, token issuance, and gaming." Supersize: "A Mini-clip style gaming platform building an onchain PVP game where token communities wager and compete". https://blog.colosseum.com/colosseums-2024-investments-and-themes-for-2025/

findings.claim: On wallet friction, Colosseum Codex promotes embedded or seedless wallets rather than dropping on-chain use. So integrate, but hide the wallet.
findings.evidence: Search-result summaries of Codex posts (not verified on the pages): wallet complexity "can be intimidating"; Phantom embedded wallets let users sign in "using just an email, Google, or Apple account"; seedless sign-in "with just an email and a four-digit PIN". https://blog.colosseum.com/breakpoint-metaplex-aura-phantom-embedded-wallets-bullet-l2/ , https://blog.colosseum.com/heaven-solanawave-swig-wallet/

findings.claim: No official source I could fetch uses the phrases 'thin blockchain use' or 'why crypto', and none describes a penalty for wallet UX friction.
findings.evidence: Searched blog.colosseum.com and colosseum.com; winner posts for Breakout, Radar, Renaissance and Cypherpunk contain no judge commentary on crypto necessity or wallets (WebFetch of each URL above).

findings.claim: All submissions also compete in the general pool whatever chain they use, so one Tempo- or Arbitrum-integrated entry can win a track prize and a general prize ($30k grand, 20 x $15k, $5k public goods). The Public Goods Award suits a shelter-payout angle.
findings.evidence: cryptobriefing: "All submissions compete within a general pool regardless of which blockchain they're built on." Rules s.14: "(b) Public Goods Award: $5,000 CASH"; "(d) An additional $15,000 CASH will be awarded to each of the next 20 standout teams". https://cryptobriefing.com/colosseum-crypto-worlds-fair-hackathon/

findings.claim: Entrants are individuals, not companies. The listed exclusions don't cover Lithuania, and there is no in-person requirement. The only relevant condition is that winning depends on sponsor due diligence.
findings.evidence: Rules s.2: "'Entrant' means an Individual"; s.13: "Winning is contingent upon the execution of Prize Acceptance Documents ... and passing of the due diligence requirements of the Administrator and/or the Contest Sponsors." s.15(b): "Each winning team may be required to set up a wallet address".

findings.claim: Scrim (Breakout 3rd, gaming) shows that on-chain money wrapped around a skill game counts. The gameplay doesn't have to run on-chain if the value flow does.
findings.evidence: "A seamless, skill-based wagering platform for competitive gamers. Built on Solana, our platform enables players to challenge" (truncated as quoted). https://colosseum.com/arena/projects/explore/scrim

research.unknowns: I couldn't find any track-specific requirements or judging text for Tempo, Arbitrum or Base. The sponsor .md files in ColosseumOrg/hackathon-resources are empty, colosseum.com/worldsfair/tempo returns 404, and arena/resources needs a login. I couldn't read the Tempo workshop content (Sayeed Mehrjerdian) or the Arbitrum/Robinhood workshop. No Tempo or Arbitrum judges are named; Base has David Tso. It's unclear whether Tempo track judges want mainnet or accept testnet. The worldsfair page shows no FAQ, so whether one entry can be tagged to several tracks at once is unconfirmed. The rules list separate Base and Robinhood Chain tracks, which the brief doesn't mention. I didn't check project pages for Maneko Pet, Moon Boi or Legends of the Sun, so how much of those games was on-chain is unverified. The wallet-friction quotes come from search summaries, not fetched pages. No past Colosseum hackathon had a Tempo or Arbitrum track, so there are no winners to compare against for those chains. The pre-window disclosure rule means the existing heist and ShelterSplit work has to be declared. How judges will weigh it against new in-window work is not stated.

research.summary:
I could not confirm that a gaming entry has ever placed at an Arbitrum Open House event. I checked the winner lists for NYC Buildathon, NYC Founder House, India Buildathon, Bengaluru Hacker House and London Founder House. Every named winner is DeFi, RWA, payments, prediction-market, privacy, insurance or AI-agent infrastructure. None is a game. The only gaming prize I found is a $1,500 "Gaming breakthrough" honorable mention at the 2025 India buildathon, and I could not identify who won it. The London online buildathon (278 submissions, $85K) listed its winners only in an X thread I could not open (HTTP 402).

The judging criteria are the same for every city: smart contract quality; product-market fit, defined as "clear potential to attract and retain users"; innovation; and real problem solving. Every page invites you to "Bring an existing project" (Dubai says "existing product"). A judge's guide (Ben Greenberg, dev.to) says traction is the tiebreaker. It counts "pilot users", "demonstrated adoption", and "evidence the project will continue to exist after the event". So yes, the criteria favour a submission tied to a product that already has users (the Token Tails web, iOS and Android app) over a brand-new standalone game. But the same sources warn against putting things on-chain for no reason ("Does it need to be onchain?") and against "'blockchain for X' pitches without clear user value". They also list payments and stablecoins, consumer products and Stylus tooling as priority sectors. Together this points to leading with the ShelterSplit USDC payout rail, deployed on Arbitrum and wired into the existing app, with Catnip Heist as the way users get in. Making the heist's gameplay itself an on-chain Arbitrum game fits the evidence less well.

Dubai is confirmed on HackQuest: online, $30K (breakdown TBD), registration Oct 31–Dec 5, submission Nov 16–Dec 6, results Dec 13, judging TBD. That is roughly a quarter of Singapore's $115K pool.

New, time-critical: the Singapore online buildathon is live now and fully online. Registration closes Oct 2, submission Oct 4, and results come Oct 12. The pool is $115K ($70K Overall, $15K Promising Products, up to $30K grants). At least one top-3 spot per track is reserved for Robinhood Chain, and there is "Extra consideration" for Paxos USDG. It is not in the planned list.

Stylus docs call it a fit for "onchain games" because memory is cheap. The $215M Gaming Catalyst Program has been rebranded to Arbitrum Gaming Ventures, which "invests" in teams. That looks like investment, which your funding rules exclude. The Stylus Sprint grants are marked complete.

findings.claim: Every Open House online buildathon uses the same four judging criteria. Product-market fit is explicitly about attracting and retaining users.
findings.evidence: "Smart contract quality — code following best practices, structured logically and efficiently, with minimal security vulnerabilities"; "Product-Market Fit — projects with clear potential to attract and retain users"; "Innovation and Creativity — original approaches that push boundaries"; "Real Problem Solving — applications that address genuine market needs" — https://www.hackquest.io/hackathons/Arbitrum-Open-House-Singapore-Online-Buildathon (identical on https://www.hackquest.io/hackathons/Arbitrum-Open-House-NYC-Online-Buildathon)

findings.claim: Existing projects are explicitly allowed. The Dubai page says 'existing product'.
findings.evidence: NYC and Singapore: "Bring an existing project or start from scratch." Dubai: "Bring an existing product or start from scratch." — https://www.hackquest.io/hackathons/Arbitrum-Open-House-Dubai-Online-Buildathon ; Singapore coverage: teams "build out an existing project or codebase while receiving feedback sessions" — https://egamers.io/singapore-is-next-for-arbitrums-open-house-115k-buildathon-kicks-off-sept-14/

findings.claim: A judge's guide says traction separates otherwise-equal teams, and counts pilot users and adoption. This favours tying the entry to the live Token Tails app, which already has users.
findings.evidence: "Two teams with similar execution and problem-solution scores get separated here." Traction = "evidence the project will continue to exist after the event"; judges assess "GitHub activity beyond the hackathon commits, social presence, community engagement, and whether there's a defined path forward"; "pilot users" and "demonstrated adoption or strong momentum with an engaged community" — Ben Greenberg for Arbitrum, Feb 17, https://dev.to/arbitrum/what-winning-arbitrum-open-house-teams-do-differently-18f8

findings.claim: The same guide values a working, tested MVP over a polished pitch, and rewards being clear on why the project needs Arbitrum specifically. It penalises generic 'blockchain for X' pitches, which argues against gratuitous on-chain gameplay.
findings.evidence: "functional MVP with decent code structure, some docs and tests, and a demo that actually works"; "Fewer still can articulate why it needs to exist on Arbitrum specifically."; "Generic DeFi dashboards and 'blockchain for X' pitches without clear user value sit near the bottom."; "a rough pitch deck with a working MVP" beats "a polished pitch deck with a broken demo" — https://dev.to/arbitrum/what-winning-arbitrum-open-house-teams-do-differently-18f8

findings.claim: Arbitrum's stated priority sectors are payments and stablecoins, DeFi, RWAs, privacy, consumer products and Stylus/Timeboost tooling. Gaming is not named. This suits ShelterSplit's USDC payouts plus the consumer app better than a standalone game.
findings.evidence: Priority sectors: "payments and stablecoins, DeFi, RWAs, privacy, consumer products, and Arbitrum-native tooling around Stylus and Timeboost" — https://dev.to/arbitrum/what-winning-arbitrum-open-house-teams-do-differently-18f8

findings.claim: Mentor advice for the Singapore buildathon asks whether the project needs to be on-chain at all.
findings.evidence: "Does it need to be onchain? If so, what unique problem does it solve?" (zkLumi/Offchain); "Double down on the foundation before adding more features" (OpenZeppelin) — https://blog.arbitrum.foundation/builders-block-025-arbitrums-buildathon-starts-next-week-heres-how-to-stand-out-in-open-house/

findings.claim: NYC Buildathon winners were Tilt Protocol, Fangorn and EqualFi. None is a game. Criteria: technical execution, product clarity, ecosystem alignment, long-term potential.
findings.evidence: Tilt Protocol $15,000, Fangorn $10,000, EqualFi $5,000; "rigorous evaluation that was based on technical execution, product clarity, ecosystem alignment, and the long-term potential of the project"; winners showed "clear user focus, promising architecture, and a clear and concise roadmap that extends beyond our Buildathon" — https://blog.arbitrum.foundation/open-house-nyc-buildathon-concludes-meet-the-winning-teams/

findings.claim: NYC Founder House awards went to Kustodia (escrow payments), Laytus (prediction markets), EqualFi (index tokens), Bond.Credit (AI underwriting) and Tilt Protocol (AI for RWAs). None is a game. Some traction evidence was cited, such as EqualFi's deployed index tokens.
findings.evidence: Kustodia 1st ($60K) "enables users to create programmable payment agreements for high-value marketplace transactions"; EqualFi: "nine index tokens have been deployed - three crypto baskets and six stock-based indices"; "473 applications; 88 teams were selected" and "55 projects submitted builds" — https://blog.arbitrum.foundation/nyc-founder-house-concludes-with-340k-in-awards-to-winning-teams/

findings.claim: London Founder House winners were all finance or AI-agent infrastructure. Live deployments (Saffron, Agama) were noted. No games.
findings.evidence: Liquida ($60K) "Regulated collateral rail for the UK's £2.7 trillion government bond market"; EdenFi ($20K) "Global money app for Africa and the diaspora"; Saffron ($60K, Robinhood Chain track), Agama Finance ($30K, "live on Robinhood Chain"); 64 projects submitted — https://blog.arbitrum.foundation/top-founders-take-home-300k-at-london-founder-house/

findings.claim: India 2025 buildathon: the podium was all DeFi or automation (Plexi, Orbital, TriggerX). There was a separate $1,500 'Gaming breakthrough' honorable mention, whose winner I could not identify.
findings.evidence: Honorable mentions "$1,500 each" including "Gaming breakthrough", "Stablecoin innovation", "Mobile solution" — https://www.hackquest.io/hackathons/Arbitrum-Open-House-India-Online-Buildathon ; winners Plexi ($15,000), Orbital ($5,000), TriggerX ($2,500); Hacker House judged on "team quality, alignment with Arbitrum, technical execution, product-market fit, and innovation" — https://blog.arbitrum.foundation/arbitrum-open-house-india-concludes-with-bengaluru-hacker-house-full-recap/

findings.claim: An India entry that shipped with real users is on the HackQuest gallery (Aristhrottle, 200+ users, live on Arbitrum One), but I found no prize for it. This shows teams do present user traction; it does not show that traction wins.
findings.evidence: "onboarded more than 200 users and have partnered with more than 10 content creators"; the page shows no prize label — https://www.hackquest.io/projects/Arbitrum-Open-House-India-Online-Buildathon-Aristhrottle

findings.claim: The only game I saw in the London HackQuest project gallery is Gauntlet, a PvP trading arena on Robinhood Chain. It is a finance-flavoured game, and I saw no winner label for it.
findings.evidence: "Gauntlet - A PvP trading arena in the browser, on Robinhood Chain. Your leveraged position is a cell in a pit" — https://arbitrum-london.hackquest.io/projects

findings.claim: Dubai buildathon is confirmed: online, $30K (breakdown TBD), submission Nov 16–Dec 6, 2026, results Dec 13. Gaming is listed as a welcome area, and Stylus or Solidity are both allowed.
findings.evidence: Registration "Oct 31, 2026 – Dec 5, 2026"; Submission "Nov 16, 2026 – Dec 6, 2026"; Reward Announcement "Dec 13, 2026"; "30,000 USD Available in Prizes"; "DeFi. Gaming. Social. Tools. Or something entirely new."; "Build with Stylus or Solidity"; "Deploy on Arbitrum One or your own Orbit chain" — https://www.hackquest.io/hackathons/Arbitrum-Open-House-Dubai-Online-Buildathon

findings.evidence: Registration "July 29, 2026 – October 2, 2026"; Submission "September 13, 2026 – October 4, 2026"; Reward "October 12, 2026"; Overall $70,000 (40/20/10K), Promising Products $15,000, grants up to $30,000; "Extra consideration is given to projects integrating Paxos' USDG stablecoin."; deploy on "Arbitrum Sepolia, Arbitrum One, or Robinhood Chain"; categories "DeFi, gaming, social applications, DePIN" — https://www.hackquest.io/hackathons/Arbitrum-Open-House-Singapore-Online-Buildathon ; Promising Products targets "teams exploring frontier territory such as AI agents and new financial primitives" — https://egamers.io/singapore-is-next-for-arbitrums-open-house-115k-buildathon-kicks-off-sept-14/

findings.evidence: "With AI making building easier, the amount of competition in buildathons has grown."; "You're using AI. No need to hide it." — https://blog.arbitrum.foundation/builders-block-026-300k-awaits-at-founder-house-singapore-what-great-startups-have-in-common/

findings.claim: The Stylus docs position Stylus as a fit for on-chain games because memory is cheap. This is the only official argument for moving heist logic on-chain, and none of the winners I found were Stylus games.

research.unknowns: I could not see the London online buildathon winner names. The thread is at https://x.com/arbitrum/status/2069113415348744568 and returned HTTP 402. I also could not identify the India "Gaming breakthrough" honorable-mention winner, and the HackQuest project-list page returned no content. openhouse.arbitrum.io returned 429 and arbitrum.io/solutions/gaming returned 403. Dubai's judging criteria and prize breakdown are marked TBD; I assume they will match the other cities' four criteria, but that is unconfirmed. I found no written Promising Products definition on HackQuest itself; the only one came from secondary press (egamers.io). I could not tell whether Arbitrum Gaming Ventures takes equity, tokens or both. I could not confirm whether the Gaming Catalyst wind-down vote passed. Judge weighting between the four criteria is not published. I have no evidence of how judges treat traction from an app's existing Web2 or mobile users versus on-chain users. Whether the team could realistically meet the Singapore deadline (register by Oct 2, deploy and submit by Oct 4) is outside what I could check.

findings.claim: Arc mainnet is live (chain 5042), and a plain injected wallet such as MetaMask can sign and send on it even without custom gas-token support. The catch is display: the gas balance may show as 'ETH'. So option (1), a donate button that calls ShelterSplit.donate(memo) with msg.value, is technically workable on Arc in a single transaction with no approve step.
findings.evidence: docs.arc.io/arc/references/connect-to-arc: "Wallets that don't support custom gas tokens still work for signing and sending transactions; balances may display as 'ETH' but the underlying token is USDC." Also "Chain ID: 5042 ... Status: Production" and "USDC as the native gas token (18 decimals)." Repo: funding/framework/tracks/a-build/shelter-split/src/ShelterSplit.sol:266 `function donate(string calldata memo) external payable nonReentrant whenNotPaused`

findings.claim: UX friction for a judge using option (1) on Arc is high even though the tech works. The judge must add a custom network by hand (Settings, Networks, Add manually), hold real USDC on Arc mainnet, and may see a confusing 'ETH' balance. Most judges will not have Arc USDC funded, so in practice they would watch a video rather than click. Estimate (J): about 4-6 AI hours for a wallet_addEthereumChain + eth_sendTransaction button with no new dependency, 1-2 human hours for funding and testing a real wallet, and medium risk (network add, decimals, the 20 gwei fee floor).
findings.evidence: docs.arc.io connect-to-arc: "Settings → Networks → Add network → Add a network manually. Enter the network name, RPC URL, chain ID (5042 or 5042002), currency symbol (USDC)...". docs.arc.io/arc/references/gas-and-fees.md: "set `maxFeePerGas` to at least 20 Gwei—transactions below this threshold may remain pending indefinitely."

findings.claim: Repo gap (a known-bug candidate to mention, not fix silently): the /shelter-payouts page decodes only the ERC-20 `Disbursed` event. Arc donate() and receive() emit `NativeDisbursed` in 18-decimal native units, while chains.ts sets Arc decimals to 6. So any donation made through the Arc donate button would NOT appear on the payouts page the heist links to. Option (1) on Arc also needs roughly 2-3 AI hours of page work: a second topic plus per-event decimals.
findings.evidence: client/components/shelter-payouts/logs.ts:4 `// keccak256("Disbursed(address,uint256,string)")` and :56 rejects other topics. ShelterSplit.sol:264 "Splits msg.value (the native coin; USDC with 18 decimals on Arc) ... Emits NativeDisbursed events." client/components/shelter-payouts/chains.ts: `5042: { name: "Arc", ... decimals: 6, symbol: "USDC" }`

findings.claim: Tempo is hostile to a naive injected-wallet donate button. For a legacy or EIP-1559 transaction that calls ShelterSplit (not a TIP-20 contract), the fee token falls back to pathUSD unless the account has set a preference. A MetaMask user holding only USDC.e would likely be unable to pay fees. disburseWithMemo is also an ERC-20 pull, so it needs an approve first (2 transactions). Fee sponsorship exists, but it needs a fee-payer service or a Tempo API key and Viem relay wiring. Risk: high.

However ... wallets should integrate Tempo Transactions, which requires switching to the type-`0x76` envelope." fee-payer: "Authenticate with a Tempo API key, then use the Fee Payer API as your sponsorship RPC URL." Repo: ShelterSplit.sol:255 `function disburseWithMemo(uint256 amount, bytes32 memo)` routes through _disburse, which reads token.balanceOf (the pull pattern).

research.summary:
Yes, it is really a case, but only in part. Putting the heist on-chain is technically possible, but the cheapest version that is safe for judges is read-only.

The four options:

- **(1) Injected-wallet donate button.** It works on Arc: MetaMask can sign even without custom gas-token support, and donate() is a single payable call. The tradeoff is friction: the judge must add the network by hand and hold Arc USDC. On Tempo it is poor: a standard transaction to ShelterSplit falls back to pathUSD for fees, and disburseWithMemo needs an approve first.
- **(2) Passkey wallet with sponsored gas.** It exists on Arc: Circle Modular (MSCA) wallets are listed for Arc, Gas Station marks Arc Mainnet as supported, and Alchemy, Dynamic, Pimlico and others are listed as AA providers. But mainnet sponsorship is charged to a developer credit card, requires ERC-4337 smart accounts, and needs a human to set up the console. Sponsorship covers gas only, not the donation itself. Estimate (J): about 12-20 AI hours, 3-5 human hours, medium-high risk.
- **(3) Read-only counter.** Lowest risk and nearly free, because the eth_getLogs machinery already exists. Estimate (J): about 3-7 AI hours, 0.5 human hours, near-zero judge friction.
- **(4) Embedding in the client.** Feasible: same three version, and App has a root element plus dispose(). But the heist uses import.meta.env.DEV unguarded, which breaks under Next unless shimmed. Estimate (J): 2-4 AI hours as a static build under client/public/heist, or 8-14 AI hours as a source embed with dynamic/ssr:false.

One concrete repo gap to mention, not fix silently: the payouts page decodes only Disbursed, not NativeDisbursed, and it uses Arc decimals of 6 while native amounts are 18. So an Arc donate() would not appear on the page that the heist win screen links to.

Recommended path (J): keep the heist standalone or served as static files, and add a read-only 'sent to shelters' counter. Keep any donate button as an optional Arc-only extra, and fix NativeDisbursed support first.
research.unknowns:
- **Circle Modular wallets:** whether Arc mainnet access needs any approval or a paid plan, and whether passkeys work inside the Capacitor iOS and Android WebViews. Neither was verified.
- **Tempo:** production Fee Payer pricing and approval were not documented. It is also unclear whether USDC.e qualifies as a fee token, and exactly what MetaMask shows on Tempo.
- **Arc wallet providers:** which of the listed AA providers support Arc mainnet was not stated.
- **Scope of checks:** hour estimates are judgment (J), not measured. The heist win-screen link is target=_blank; I did not check the full link attributes. I did not run the heist build under Next to confirm the import.meta failure; that conclusion comes from reading the code. WebFetch summaries paraphrase some pages, so the verbatim quotes are only as exact as the fetch model returned them.

research.summary: I found no precedent where a game won a hackathon or grant because it made on-chain charity donations inside the game. The closest winners are narrow. SpaceTombo, a "gamified lucky draw game... to fund charitable organizations", won Chainlink's $15k NFT prize in 2021. Onda, which sends automatic $0.01 USDC micropayments to artists, won an Arc track at ETHGlobal Cannes 2026. Charity Connect won in Base Onchain Summer's "Unplugged" track. PetsFundMe, a pet-donation project, collected only ETHOnline 2022 sponsor pool prizes, and Charity Casino shows no prize. Recent winners at Arc, Circle and Colosseum are mostly infrastructure (FX DEX, treasury, x402 or MCP payment rails, agent payments) plus "real problems" apps. Judges rewarded two kinds of things: stablecoin payments where the chain is hidden from the user, and verifiable proof (deployed contracts, public repos, traction). Charity and games are not a stated priority at Circle or Tempo. Circle's 2026 grant categories are agentic activity, stablecoin FX, peer-to-peer payments, treasury, prediction markets and lending. Its first 2026 grant cohort is all "production-grade systems". Tempo's stated use cases include "Global payouts", "Microtransactions" and memos "for payment reconciliation". So judges would score a real payout that is verifiable on-chain and uses memos; the game itself scores little. The best-supported position is a middle one: the heist should trigger or link to a real ShelterSplit payment (this is what Onda did and won), without on-chain game logic or token mechanics. On eligibility, secondary sources say Arc Microgrants requires a live Arc mainnet deployment (mainnet went live 2026-09-16) and a public repo, and that testnet-only builds are ineligible. So ShelterSplit must be on Arc mainnet, not testnet, by the Oct 7 submission (the program closes Oct 14).

verdict.claimHolds:
Partly. The direction is right, but the Colosseum figure is too high for anything you can safely ship by Oct 11, and "Arc unchanged" is slightly wrong.

- **Colosseum:** +1 for Tempo and about +0.5 for Arbitrum/general is defensible. +2 is not, unless the heist shows or triggers a real Tempo memo payout during the window, and the Tempo wallet path is the riskiest build on the list. Most of the Colosseum gain comes from ShelterSplit being deployed on Tempo and Arbitrum. The heist mostly adds the story and a way in for users.
- **Dubai:** +1 to +1.5 holds. The gain comes from linking the heist to the live app that already has users (option 4), plus the required Arbitrum deploy. Putting the gameplay on-chain adds nothing here.
- **Arc:** not unchanged. It is +0.5 with the counter, and up to +1 if an Arc-only donate button works on mainnet. A broken demo is about -2.
- **Team1 and Circle:** unchanged, which matches your claim. No evidence covers Team1, and Circle's grant categories leave out games and charity.
- **Anitya:** unchanged at best. Wiring the game on-chain only adds risk for a game jam.
verdict.recommendation:
Don't put gameplay on-chain, and don't make judges use a wallet. Ship three things:

1. **A read-only "sent to shelters" counter on the win screen (option 3).** Before it, fix the payouts decoder so it reads NativeDisbursed events and uses the right decimals per event.
2. **A public static deploy of the heist, then a copy under client/public/heist linked from the Token Tails app (option 4a).**
3. **A real payout on Tempo using disburseWithMemo, with a memo that names the heist campaign.** The counter shows it, which gives Colosseum Tempo judges an on-chain action they can inspect without holding a wallet.

An injected-wallet donate button on Arc (option 1) is a stretch goal only. It needs the decoder fix to have landed first and needs to be working by Oct 4.

Skip these before Oct 12, and revisit the passkey wallet for Dubai in November:
- option 1 on Tempo;
- option 2 (passkey wallet with sponsored gas);
- option 4b (embedding the heist source in the client).

Two extra points:
- Don't add a per-win write path to back payouts with win counts. CLAUDE.md allows game scores to be written only through POST /user/catbassadors/live. Keep the memo payout a campaign payout that the team funds.
- The decoder gap is a known bug. Mention it and fix it as its own deliberate change, not as a side effect of other work.

The injected-wallet path on Tempo is hostile: fees fall back to pathUSD and the pull needs an approve first. So the realistic gain comes from a memo payout judges can verify, not from a wallet in the game. The 7.5 is the one estimate you gave for the whole entry, and the deltas are my judgment. It is unknown whether the Tempo track wants mainnet.

Today an Arc donation would not show on the payouts page (it decodes only Disbursed and assumes 6 decimals), so a half-built button costs points. Linking the heist to the app that already has users is the lever, together with the required Arbitrum deploy. No past winner was a game. Dubai's criteria and prize split are still TBD.
There is no evidence at all on what Team1 wants. The Avalanche ShelterSplit deploy is what counts. Any heist delta would be invented.

You gave no baseline, so the 0 means not estimated, not a 0% chance. The 2026 categories are agentic payments, FX, P2P, treasury, prediction markets and lending. The first cohort was all 'production-grade systems'. Games and charity don't fit, so heist wiring changes nothing, and passkey wallets won't make it fit.
Game jams are judged on the game. None of the research covered Anitya's rules, so there is no evidence that wallets help. Wallet friction during a jam playtest is only downside.

verdict.keyEvidence:
Colosseum:
- Rules s.8(d) score how well the entry uses blockchain for UX.
- s.14 defines each track as integrating with that chain.
- None of the 26 gaming and consumer winners checked was a purely off-chain game. Scrim shows that on-chain money around an off-chain skill game can count.

Arbitrum:
- The criteria ask for product-market fit, meaning attracting and retaining users.
- The judge guide uses traction as the tiebreaker and warns against 'blockchain for X' pitches.
- None of the named winners was a game.

Arc:
- Mainnet is live, and injected wallets can sign.
- Microgrants reportedly requires an Arc mainnet component (search snippet only).

Tempo:
- Fees fall back to pathUSD, so a standard donate transaction fails for a wallet holding only USDC.e.
- The stated use cases are payouts and memos.

Circle:
- The 2026 grant categories leave out games and charity.

Repo facts I checked:
- client/components/shelter-payouts/logs.ts:56 rejects any log that isn't Disbursed.
- chains.ts:15 sets Arc to 6 decimals.
- catnip-heist/src/ui/ui.ts:129 and :682 hold the payoutsUrl link.
- catnip-heist/src/app/App.ts:189 and src/main.ts:38 read import.meta.env.DEV unguarded.
- git shows catnip-heist and shelter-split first committed on 2026-09-29, inside the Colosseum window.
verdict.weakSpots:
- **P deltas are my judgment.** No source puts a number on the effect of heist wiring.
- **Colosseum baseline.** The 7.5% covers one entry, not each track separately.
- **Colosseum track rules.** There are no Tempo or Arbitrum track criteria, no named judges, and no mainnet rule, and there are no past Tempo winners to compare against.
- **In-window credit.** The git dates suggest the heist is in-window work, which cuts against the research's claim that the 8 levels earn little credit. But a first commit date is not proof of when development started, and any earlier work must be disclosed.
- **Arc and Circle wallets.** The Arc testnet exclusion comes from a search snippet only. Circle mainnet access and whether passkeys work in the Capacitor WebViews are unverified.
- **Untested build.** The claim that import.meta breaks under Next comes from reading the code, not from running a build.
- **Dubai.** The criteria and prize split are TBD.
- **Coverage gaps.** There is no evidence at all for Team1 or Anitya.
- **Hours.** All estimates are judgment.
- **Missing from the plan.** The Arbitrum Singapore online buildathon ($115K) closes registration Oct 2 and submission Oct 4. It is not in the plan and would clash with the Arc work.
